title: Design and study of the electron beam-line at the European XFEL (ELBEX) for strong field quantum electro-dynamics
summary: Quantum electro-dynamic (QED) processes have been studied in the perturbative regime, well below the Schwinger limit. Exploring QED above this limit would require electric fields only obtainable in the lab frame with Lorentz boosting. Laser Und XFEL Experiment (LUXE) is an international project that aims to collide the 17.5 GeV electrons of the European XFEL with a high-power laser, allowing the study of non-linear Compton scattering, non-linear Breit-Wheeler pair creation and non-linear Trident process. The electron beam line at the European XFEL (ELBEX) project aims to provide the electron beam for LUXE and two other experiments. This project will be in the currently unused XTD8 tunnel of the EuXFEL and a new transport beam line must be designed. From the existing beam path, it will extract specific bunches and focus the transverse beam sizes at the needed locations for the experiments. Using the accelerator tracking code Xsuite, an achromatic and isochronous beam line was designed. There are two main phenomena that can impact the measured signal at LUXE. The first one is the background particles reaching the detectors, coming from the beam interactions with the residual gas and the beam pipe. Background simulations realized with the Geant4 based software BDSIM showed that there was not significant impact on the LUXE IP background rates. The second phenomena are the variations in electron bunches properties, i.e. beam jitter. Measurements at the EuXFEL are performed to evaluate the jitter for various beam parameters. Electron-laser collision simulations performed with Ptarmigan showed that beam size jitter is the only parameter with major impact on the signal at LUXE. The compact linear accelerator for research and applications (CLARA) facility is also looking at the possibilities of QED interactions by colliding a 250 MeV electron beam with 100 TW laser pulses.

title: Fast prediction of electron-beam parameters using transfer maps and machine learning in a digital model of a MeV $γγ$ collider
summary: Tuning the electron beam of a MeV-scale $γγ$ collider, first in the design and later in a digital twin of the machine, requires the beam parameters at the interaction point (IP) for many injector states. Start-to-end particle tracking is too slow for this and needs the full particle distribution, which an operating machine cannot measure. We address this problem for the 200-MeV transport line of the collider with two fast predictors. For design, second-order transfer maps from the transport entrance to the IP are applied to every particle. For a digital twin, an extremely-randomized-trees (ExtraTrees) model predicts the IP parameters from the means and rms widths of the beam at the transport entrance. On 89 held-out start-to-end simulations, the map predictor reproduces Elegant tracking for the mean energy, momentum spread, bunch length, transverse rms sizes and normalized emittances with coefficients of determination ($R^2$) of 0.97--1.00 and is ten times faster. The ExtraTrees model reaches an average $R^2$ of 0.88, compared with 0.58 when the injector settings are used as input, and performs similarly with eleven inputs that can be measured or reconstructed. Under a 2% input perturbation, the average $R^2$ of the six parameters other than the mean energy decreases only from 0.917 to 0.895, whereas the mean energy requires an accurate momentum calibration. The two predictors provide the IP-beam evaluation for the collider design and the prediction layer of a future digital twin.

title: Quantum transport of vortex electrons in bending magnets and circular accelerators
summary: Controlling the sizes and phase structure of single-particle wave packets in accelerators remains an experimental challenge and requires understanding how bending magnets transform these states. An important example is transporting relativistic vortex electrons through the magnets to a collision point while keeping a narrow orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) distribution. We derive an effective Hamiltonian that accounts for the packet acceleration, employ it to obtain a generalized BMT-like equation, match the electron state at both magnet boundaries, and calculate the mean OAM and its variance. A half turn can reverse the mean OAM relative to the momentum while broadening its distribution, so recovering the mean does not ensure state recovery. We identify windows in packet sizes and bend angles for a small OAM spread and show that weak bends can produce narrow distributions with the mean OAM tilted relative to the momentum, making these states candidates for spatiotemporal vortices. For a few MeV electrons, we propose to use half-turn magnets that leave the mean OAM nearly antiparallel to the momentum while keeping its distribution narrow. For a circular orbit in a uniform field, the OAM variance after the exit grows as $N^2$ over $N$ turns, favoring linear accelerators, such as LINAC at JINR, for first experiments in MeV range.

title: Atomic Static Electric Quadrupole Polarizability from Relativistic Many-Body Theory With Application To Thulium $\left(6s^2\, 4f^{13}\right)$\, $^2F_{7/2}$ and $^2F_{5/2}$
summary:
In the present work a method for calculating atomic static electric rank-$n$ tensor quadrupole polarizabilities $α_Q^{(n)}(J)$ for arbitrary atomic electronic structure is presented. It is based on a linear-symmetry representation of atomic states using large-scale relativistic configuration interaction wavefunctions, and the quadrupole polarizabilities are obtained by a sum-over-states approach.
  The major result from applying this method to atomic thulium is $α_Q^{(0)}(\frac{7}{2}) = 2496^{+0}_{-231}$ \au for the electronic ground term $^2F_{7/2}$ static electric scalar quadrupole polarizability which is roughly a factor of four smaller than same property in the electronic ground state of the cesium atom. This finding adds to the favorable properties of thulium atoms in atomic-clock research.

title: Closed analytical formulas for the Ashley-Ritchie-Brandt and Jackson-McCarthy polarization functions
summary: The $Z_{1}^{3}$ correction in the Bethe-Bloch formula that quantifies the electronic stopping power of matter for heavy charged particles is revisited. This correction accounts for the Barkas-Andersen effect. Ashley, Ritchie and Brandt (ARB) wrote it in terms of a non-relativistic polarization function, and Jackson and McCarthy (JM) obtained the relativistic counterpart. Both expressions involve intricate triple integrals. The present manuscript describes how the polarization functions of JM and ARB can be reduced to compact analytical formulas. The corresponding asymptotic behaviours are also found. The accuracy of two currently-used empirical fits to the ARB and JM polarization functions is assessed.

title: Atomic Parity Violation: Standard Model Tests
comment: Chapter in Encyclopedia of Particle Physics, 1st Edition, Elsevier
summary: Atomic parity violation (APV) offers a sensitive high-precision, low-energy test of the Standard Model and a powerful probe of new physics. It played a significant role in confirming the nature of the neutral weak currents, and gives unique information about fundamental weak parameters and possible new physics, reaching energies well into the TeV scale and beyond. In this chapter, we provide a pedagogical introduction to the fascinating field of APV. The underlying mechanisms are introduced, an overview of past and ongoing experiments is presented, including prospects for measuring parity violation in molecules, and the critical role of electronic structure theory in interpreting the experiments is described. The importance of the nuclear anapole moment and other nuclear-spin-dependent parity-violating contributions for understanding nuclear structure and weak nuclear forces is highlighted. We discuss the current challenges and identify the most important and pressing goals in this field, which promises exciting discoveries in the coming years.

title: Spectrotemporal imaging of ultrafast electron dynamics
summary: We demonstrate a spectrotemporal imaging technique that maps ultrafast electron dynamics onto energy- and angle-resolved photoelectron distributions in a single measurement. The underlying principle is to encode the probing time into the kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons, while the evolving quantum dynamics is retrieved from their angular distributions. We experimentally demonstrate this concept by imaging spin-orbit wave packet dynamics in resonance-enhanced multiphoton ionization of potassium atoms using two complementary approaches. In the first, three spectrally distinct probe pulses sample the dynamics at selected delays and map the corresponding wave packet configurations onto separate photoelectron energy channels. In the second, a single broadband chirped probe pulse establishes a continuous time-to-energy mapping through its time-dependent instantaneous frequency, thereby encoding the evolution of the wave packet across a broad photoelectron energy band. The resulting photoelectron momentum distribution exhibits a characteristic fork-shaped pattern. Combining supercontinuum pulse shaping with velocity map imaging, we experimentally resolve the spin-orbit dynamics over a time window exceeding 300 fs, in good agreement with quantum dynamical simulations. Our results establish spectrotemporal photoelectron imaging as a versatile approach to time-resolved spectroscopy, replacing sequential delay scans by parallel acquisition of ultrafast quantum dynamics.

title: Atomic Transition Rates on a Quantum Annealer
summary: Electric-dipole (E1) transition rates underlie applications across many areas of physics and demand more accurate wavefunctions than ground-state energies do. We report the first calculation of E1 transition rates on a D-Wave quantum annealer, for neutral Li, Li-like Be, neutral Na, and Na-like Mg. We use a zooming-and-sigma-annealing scheme with floating-point encoding within the Quantum Annealer Eigensolver (QAE) algorithm, which yields ground-state eigenvectors accurate to the chosen three decimal places. Treating the lowest even-parity ($^2S_{1/2}$) and odd-parity ($^2P_{1/2}$, $^2P_{3/2}$) states as separate angular-symmetry sectors gives QAE access to excited atomic configurations for transition-rate calculations. Our results reproduce relativistic configuration-interaction values obtained classically to within numerical precision, demonstrating that the QAE framework extends to a broader class of atomic properties on near-term quantum hardware.

title: Bringing Dark States to Light after Frustrated Tunneling Ionization
summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in gases is typically regarded as a sub-laser-cycle process, well described by the semiclassical three-step model. In this work, we report the extreme-ultraviolet (XUV) emission observed in an HHG experiment arising from a longer temporal process associated with dark states populated through frustrated tunneling ionization. The emission exhibits a larger spatial divergence than typical high-order harmonics, resembling the polarization decay of optically bright states. Supported by the time-frequency analysis of the theoretical calculations, we show that the emission originates from the nonradiative capture of the tunneling electrons into excited dark states of the neutral atom, followed by Floquet-like laser-dressing effects induced by the extended tail of the driving pulse. Our results reveal a largely unexplored pathway for XUV generation through laser-dressed dark states, thereby enabling the enhancement of coherent XUV emission at targeted wavelengths with high repetition rates.

title: Charge-Reversal-Based Extraction of Muonic Ions
summary: Negative muon capture in matter is accompanied by Auger electron emission and the formation of positively charged muonic ions. This charge reversal provides a possibility for electromagnetic extraction of the products of muon capture. Here we propose a charge-reversal-based extraction scheme for muonic ions, in which negative muons are moderated and confined in a dilute gas environment before conversion, and the resulting muonic ions are subsequently accelerated and extracted by electrostatic fields. The feasibility of the concept is investigated through order-of-magnitude estimates of the competing processes, including muon moderation, muonic-ion formation, charge exchange, and acceleration in the gas medium. A magnetic-electrostatic deceleration scheme is proposed to reduce the transverse phase space of practical low-energy muon beams while retaining controlled longitudinal motion, and is directly matched to the electrostatic capture region. The analysis indicates that muonic-ion formation and extraction within the muon lifetime are not excluded by fundamental timescale constraints, although the quantitative efficiency remains uncertain because several relevant low-energy cross sections and charge-state populations are poorly constrained experimentally.

title: Certifying the Rydberg-exposure limit of a globally driven controlled-Z gate
summary: Rydberg excitation enables entangling gates in neutral-atom quantum processors but also exposes them to spontaneous decay. Whether this exposure can be made arbitrarily small through pulse shaping and longer gate times has remained unresolved. We show that an exact controlled-$Z$ gate driven by a single global laser has an irreducible Rydberg-exposure cost in the perfect-blockade regime. The product of the maximum Rabi frequency $Ω_{\max}$ and the average time $T_R$ spent in the Rydberg state is bounded below by $2.9312$, independent of pulse shape and duration. We derive this bound using a sum-of-squares certificate, strengthened by constraints imposed by the shared drive. Using interval arithmetic, we also certify the existence of an exact gate pulse with $Ω_{max} T_R<2.9359$. The unrounded bounds differ by less than $0.16\%$. The bound identifies a fundamental cost of shared-drive entangling dynamics and establishes a benchmark against which future gate-control strategies can be assessed.

title: A physics-based-preconditioned quasi-Newton solver for energy- and momentum-conserving implicit hybrid particle-in-cell simulations
summary: Explicit hybrid particle-in-cell (PIC) schemes, with kinetic ions and fluid electrons, accumulate numerical heating over long simulations and are unstable to finite-grid instabilities. Energy-conserving implicit integration removes heating and instabilities, but may be inefficient due to the need of nonlinear iteration. We present a fast quasi-Newton solver for an implicit hybrid-PIC formulation. The nonlinear residual employs the electric field and electron pressure as nonlinear unknowns, and nonlinearly eliminates particles. The formulation is strictly energy conserving and, on Cartesian meshes, also momentum conserving. The nonlinear iteration is efficiently performed with a quasi-Newton solver that replaces the true Jacobian with an approximate one without spoiling conservation properties upon convergence. The approximate Jacobian replaces the particle ion linear response with an analytical mass matrix that is local and requires minimal storage. This approximate Jacobian is efficiently inverted with a physics-based multigrid preconditioner, adapted from Hall MHD. We verify the scheme linearly with whistler, kinetic Alfvén, and cylindrical normal modes, and nonlinearly with the GEM reconnection challenge. On GEM, explicit integration needs a forty-times-smaller time step, and nine times the wall-clock time, to reach an energy conservation comparable to that of the implicit solver. We apply the method to the simulation of a three-dimensional field-reversed configuration formation by external coils.

title: A componentwise spherical Dirichlet-to-Neumann closure for finite-volume MHD at finite magnetic Reynolds number
summary: At finite magnetic Reynolds number, the field induced by a moving conducting fluid or solid extends into open space, so a finite mesh needs an outer boundary condition that represents the decaying exterior field. Magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) codes widely use pseudo-vacuum or truncation at a finite radius. Neither condition is physically correct for a vacuum exterior, but the exact alternatives are costly or limited to simple geometries. We present a Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) closure on a fixed enclosing sphere and release it as part of the open-source multi-region finite-volume solver FreeMHD. The closure matches each Cartesian component of the vector potential to its decaying exterior solution, which retains all three decaying vector-Laplace families. A meshed vacuum buffer connects non-spherical conductors to the sphere. We verify the closure with manufactured modes, sphere free decay, sphere and oblate dynamos, and a freely braking rotor. Under refinement, oblate dynamo thresholds and sphere growth rates converge toward independent spectral references, and the rotor torque matches an exact transient reference. On the same sphere, pseudo-vacuum and truncation give the larger errors predicted by their exterior models.

title: The lattice Boltzmann machine
summary: The lattice Boltzmann (LB) method is widely regarded as a very flexible and efficient solver for a broad class of transport phenomena in fluids, soft matter and related fields. In this paper, we posit that such flexibility is a direct result of its generative nature as a rule-driven information-processing machine. Its update, a relaxation toward a local target followed by a shift along the lattice, belongs to the same class of iterated relaxation dynamics as residual networks and transformers, with the difference that in LB the operators are fixed by conservation and symmetry rather than learned from data. We show that three properties of this update are sufficient to promote the emergence of closed macroscopic laws from the underlying iteration process, the physical content of the target deciding the specific law in question. A machine whose target is drawn at random generates the transport law predicted from its moments. A network given the same three properties on a graph, where there is no lattice, is trained on a traffic process and generates a conservation law of its own. The mechanism has a precise limit, where the damping of the non-conserved modes fails, and on the lattice the macroscopic law gives no warning of it. In this reading, LB is a lattice Boltzmann machine whose informing rules are supplied by physics rather than by training. Its three properties then state what a new ingredient should preserve when it enters an LB model, whether it comes from physics or from data.

title: Low-Rank Tensor Manifolds for Turbulent Field Reconstruction from Sparse Data
summary: Reconstructing turbulent flow fields from sparse and irregular measurements remains challenging because the underlying inverse problem is severely underdetermined. Here we present MANTRA, a manifold-based tensor framework that represents each velocity component in a continuous tensor-product space while constraining its coefficient tensor to a low-rank Tucker manifold. This structure provides a compact, data-adaptive representation without requiring gridded observations or governing equations. Riemannian optimization and adaptive selection of rank and basis complexity enable the model to exploit coordinate-wise spatiotemporal correlations. In simulations of forced isotropic turbulence and flow over a cylinder, MANTRA recovers multiscale structures at sampling densities orders of magnitude below the underlying grids and remains accurate under Gaussian noise up to 20% of the peak velocity. It also recovers leading coordinate-wise correlation structures from sparse observations. Applied to experimental particle-tracking velocimetry of an oscillating impinging jet, MANTRA reveals time-evolving structures that are not apparent from the scattered measurements alone.

title: Hydrodynamic interaction in Lattice Fokker Planck for dilute polymer dynamics
summary: We extend the BGK-type kinetic model for polymer dumbbells and its lattice Boltzmann implementation by incorporating hydrodynamic interaction (HI) effects to accurately recover the slow-variable dynamics governed by the Smoluchowski equation. Unlike Brownian dynamics approaches, which demand the computationally expensive evaluation of the square root of the configuration-dependent diffusion tensor at every time step, this kinetic method is straightforward to implement and avoids such overhead entirely. Consequently, it achieves a significant reduction in computational cost. We validate the model in steady and transient shear flows, demonstrating its ability to capture the distinct signatures of hydrodynamic interactions on bulk rheological properties.

title: Extensions to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier Equations for Rarefied Transport: Entropy Variable Formulation, Heat Transfer and Dispersion of a Non-Linear Entropy Stable Closure
summary: We assess the non-linear version of the Entropy Stable Extension to the Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations which were originally derived in arXiv:2407.17334. Using an identity for the derivative of the inverse of linearized collision operator, we show that the Entropy Stable Extension takes the form of a fourth-order quasi-cubic system of equations when written in entropy variables. Furthermore, we find that the quasi-linear contributions to the extension retain the highest order derivative contributions and the entropy stability of the full extension. This quasi-linear approximation is applied to the stationary heat transfer between parallel plates where we find that a specification of the boundary conditions that interpolates between the continuum and collisions limits can yield temperature profiles that better agree with DSMC predictions than Navier-Stokes-Fourier equations with Smoluchowski boundary conditions, while also giving a heat flux prediction that better agrees with the Sherman-Lees heat flux than the Navier-Stokes-Fourier prediction. We conclude with a brief study of dispersion of plane waves according to the linearized equations in one dimension where we show that all frequency modes are stable and relate this to entropy stability.

title: Winding-Pack Quench Simulation of Stellarator Coils: Hydraulic Field-Network Coupling and Transverse Heat Conduction in OPENSC$^2$
comment: 31 pages, 24 figures, 2 tables. Submitted for publication in Superconductor Science and Technology
summary: Quench propagation in cable-in-conduit conductors is thermo-hydraulically driven, yet existing 1D models treat a conductor as one straight adiabatic cable with prescribed pressure and mass-flow boundaries, so secondary quenches and flow redistribution between windings cannot be resolved. We extend the open-source code OPENSC$^2$ with transverse heat conduction between turns, a 3D field resolving the current-sharing temperature, induced losses, and a lumped hydraulic network coupled to the conductors by a mass-flow formulation. Validated against the 2006 W7-X coil tests, it predicts the quench site, cuts the outlet-temperature error from 55 K to 12 K, and reproduces the neighboring windings' heating as flow reversal through the coil inlet.

title: Orientation and slip statistics of spheroids settling in turbulence
summary: Small spheroids settling through turbulence are turned broadside-on by fluid inertia and tilted away by velocity gradients. We describe their orientation and slip statistics through the crossover from random orientation to alignment, in the overdamped limit. With quasi-static Stokes drag the leading inertial torque is an exact gradient flow on the orientation sphere, its potential quadratic in the cosine of the tilt and only rescaled by mobility anisotropy. The orientation performs an overdamped random walk in a quadratic well, and isotropic Gaussian white noise gives exactly a Boltzmann distribution. For forcing of finite correlation time, a closure keeps this form with its width set by linear response; it recovers the uniform density as settling vanishes and, for fixed-orientation forcing statistics, the aligned coefficient of rapid-settling theory, and errs most in the crossover. The root-mean-square lateral slip peaks where the alignment rate approaches the Kolmogorov rate, as faster settling strengthens the sideways drift at a given tilt but suppresses the tilt; the nearly shape-independent ratio, which tensor-forced simulations reproduce, lets a measured peak constrain the torque coefficient or dissipation rate for given forcing statistics. Dissipation intermittency enters as a lognormal superposition of Boltzmann distributions, which fattens the tails but leaves the leading aligned mean-square tilt unchanged. The superposition reproduces the shape of plate orientation distributions from direct numerical simulations, where a single Boltzmann distribution fails; published moments confirm the predicted spread beyond the weakest torques, and at strong alignment the measured fourth-order tilt moment lies between the two predictions.

title: Quantifying the remaining search space in analogue optimisation
summary: Benchmarking analogue optimisers requires certifying not only how close a returned energy is to the optimum, but also how many better configurations may remain. Semidefinite relaxations provide rigorous bounds on the ground-state energy and selected observables, yet reveal little about the size of this residual search space. We introduce a deterministic, instance-specific upper bound on the number of binary configurations whose energies improve upon a returned state by a prescribed margin. Combined with a semidefinite energy interval, this yields a complementary certificate of both the magnitude and multiplicity of any possible improvement. To judge an analogue optimiser's native performance, we provide a generalisation of the framework to obtain bounds on the Haar volume of the remaining continuous phase-space. To further characterise the remaining search space, we extend our bounds to resolve regions in configuration space in both the binary and continuous setting. Our approach couples a variational-Chernoff reduction with an elimination bound of the resulting partition function. Comparisons with exact enumeration and independent Haar sampling are consistent with the bounds on small instances. In numerical experiments at $N=1000$, even the largest family-median bound restricts the potentially improving binary configurations to less than $10^{-144}$ of the full configuration space, while the largest upper bound on the corresponding Haar volume is of order $10^{-499}$.

title: Bouncing or Merging in Drop-Bath Impacts
comment: 45 pages, 19 figures. Submitted to the Journal of Fluid Mechanics
summary: When a liquid drop impacts a liquid surface, it deforms the surface, trapping a thin layer of air between drop and bath. The drop then either bounces off the bath or, if the gas film ruptures, merges with it. We present a model for drop-bath impacts that can accurately predict whether a drop will bounce or merge, and compare it to theory-driven experiments. The model incorporates a lubrication description of the deforming trapped gas film, which accounts for its significant curvature, within a finite-element framework. Capturing this outcome requires micro- and nano-scale physics: van der Waals-driven disjoining pressure and gas-kinetic effects that depend on the mean free path of the gas. Using only independently measured material parameters, we obtain the first quantitative agreement with experiment for the critical impact speed separating bounce from merge. We explore the behaviour of drop-bath impacts at low ambient air pressure, and then investigate the bounce-merge threshold for impacts onto shallow baths and thin films, finding a bounce-merge-bounce-merge transition as the bath depth decreases.

title: Deep-learning surrogate model for rapid quantum-noise computation in dual-pump fiber-optic phase-sensitive amplifiers
summary: Fiber-optic parametric amplifiers in a phase-sensitive amplifier (PSA) configuration are well known for their low noise properties. Quantum mechanics dictates that these amplifiers can have a 0 dB noise figure (NF) (ratio of signal-to-noise ratio at the input and output of the amplifier) under certain conditions. However, for a dual-pump configuration, when the system is highly nonlinear, fully quantum calculations of NF become non-trivial. In such cases, semi-quantum models of NF evaluation exists, however, they are often complicated and resource intensive. To simplify that, in this work, first we use a semi-quantum NF calculation framework for the generation of numerically simulated input-output dataset of NF over a large parameter spaces. Then we use the data to train an optimized deep neural network (DNN) for rapid NF prediction. Utilizing the DNN, we demonstrate about 400 times reduction in the computation time compared to the standard semi-quantum NF evaluation approach with a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.0015 dB. Using clustering we demonstrate a rapid exploration of the parameter space with respect to high gain (20 dB) and low NF (0.3 dB) targets and retrieve associated design parameters. These results illustrate the efficacy of machine learning-based approaches for rapid search of high-dimensional parameter spaces especially in compute intensive photonic systems.

title: A Study of Side Jet Interactions over a Hypersonic Cone Flow using Kinetic Methods
comment: Accepted manuscript. Published in AIAA Journal 61, 4741-4751 (2023). DOI: 10.2514/1.J063020. Partially presented at AIAA Aviation 2022 (AIAA 2022-3987) and AIAA SCITECH 2023 (AIAA 2023-0857)
summary: The interaction between the hypersonic flow over a cone and a side jet creates complex multiple recirculation regions as well as separation, reattachment and bow shocks known as Edney-Type IV shock-shock interactions. The interactions between these multi-scale structures are shown to be well captured with the direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) method, a particle-kinetic approach. This computational technique was used because even though the free stream conditions were continuum-like, sufficiently strong gradients in the shock and jet expansion were observed to cause continuum breakdown. The time-accurate DSMC approach has been shown in previous work to capture the multi-scale structures and unsteadiness in the shock structure that occurs in such flows, as was also observed in this work. These sources of unsteadiness in the shock system are shown to locally affect surface parameters such as heat transfer and skin friction as well as predict a low frequency unsteadiness consistent with earlier values in the literature.

title: Modeling the wall-normal velocity spectra in channel flow
summary: A model is proposed for the wall-normal Reynolds stress and its one-dimensional spectrum in channel flows. The model is tested for friction Reynolds numbers from 550 to 5200. The formulation for the stress is a simple modification of the one devised for boundary layers by Kunkel & Marusic (J. Fluid Mech. 548, 2006), and holds for $y/δ< 0.75$. The model for the spectrum holds for all wall distances. It is constructed in wavenumber space, and comprises two principal contributions to the spectrum: energy-containing motions and viscous-dominated motions. It is in accord with the attached eddy model where that applies, and the viscous contribution scales on the Kolmogorov length and velocity. Its extension to boundary layers, with no change to the constants, appears promising, including at Reynolds numbers well above those of the channel data.

title: Reprogrammable polaritonic skyrmion and meron lattices based on the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$
summary: Optical topological quasiparticles such as skyrmions and merons consist of engineered electromagnetic fields which can be realized via the controlled interference of polaritons. The resulting polaritonic topological lattices offer a promising platform for on-chip information encoding and nanoscale light-matter interaction. However, realizing these functionalities requires active tailoring of the polaritonic topological lattice. Although previous works have achieved tuning of the size of the polaritonic lattice sites, these methods relied on cumbersome and time-consuming fabrication processes and do not allow reconfiguration of the topological invariant. Here, we demonstrate fast optical prototyping of reconfigurable hexagonal and square coupling structures for the generation of polaritonic topological lattices with hyperbolic phonon polaritons in hBN using the phase-change material In$_3$SbTe$_2$. As In$_3$SbTe$_2$ can be switched reversibly between its dielectric ($\varepsilon$>0) amorphous and metallic ($\varepsilon$<0) crystalline phase by laser pulses, metallic In$_3$SbTe$_2$ coupling structures can be optically programmed and reconfigured. Our approach enables tailoring the size of the topological lattice sites by tuning the incident frequency. Moreover, In$_3$SbTe$_2$ allows for tailoring the topological invariant by reprogramming the coupling structure. Our platform enables reprogramming of robust optical topologies within minutes, opening a route toward rewritable on-chip photonic computing based on robust and on demand reconfigurable topological states.

title: Continuous Space-Time Finite Element Simulations for Biomedical Flows with Large Boundary Motion and Time-Periodicity
summary: We present an axisymmetric continuous simplex space-time finite element method for incompressible fluid flow. Compared to conventional time-stepping methods, the space-time approach has several advantages. First, the motion of the domain is incorporated into the space-time geometry, allowing for large boundary motion without remeshing or projection of the solution. Second, the method allows for time-periodic solutions to be computed directly, without the need to simulate multiple cycles. Third, the space-time mesh can be partitioned in time as well as in space, which enables parallelism in time. The method is demonstrated on an intra-aortic balloon pump (IABP) in a rigid tube. The balloon inflation is modelled based on measured data, and includes a travelling wave along the balloon. The method is able to resolve complex flow features such as jets and recirculation zones. A refinement study shows convergence under temporal, spatial and combined space-time refinement. In weak scaling tests up to 960 ranks, the cost per solver iteration remains approximately constant, and partitioning the mesh into time slabs improves the convergence of the linear solver compared to partitions that cut through both space and time.

title: On the aerodynamics of an accelerating and decelerating propeller in hover at low Reynolds numbers
summary: Small unmanned aerial vehicles commonly regulate propeller thrust through rapid changes in rotational speed, yet it remains unclear how the inflow, the wake, and the near-surface velocity respond to these changes at low Reynolds numbers. A commercial two-bladed propeller was tested in hover with custom blade holders at three additional pitch offsets relative to the original blade geometry, $Θ=\,$0, 5, and $10^\circ$, and accelerated and decelerated between 3000 and 5000 RPM with open-loop step responses. The resulting nondimensional acceleration and deceleration numbers, below 0.011 and 0.007, suggest negligible acceleration effects. Phase-locked particle image velocimetry (PIV) at 40, 60, and $80\,\%$ rotor radius and in the meridian plane was combined with load measurements. The thrust coefficient responds quasi-steadily at $Θ= 10^\circ$, but shows hysteresis at the higher pitch offsets, with lower values during acceleration and higher values during deceleration than under steady conditions. This trend opposes expectations from dynamic inflow theory. The effect is largest at $Θ= 5^\circ$, with deviations from the steady values of up to 8\,% during acceleration and $5\,\%$ during deceleration, compared with $4\,\%$ and $3\,\%$ at $Θ= 10^\circ$. PIV reveals that the rotor-disk inflow, blade deformation, and sectional circulation remain largely quasi-steady, whereas velocity fluctuations, blade-wake vorticity, and tip-vortex circulation vary strongly, with the largest deviations at low rotational speeds rather than at peak acceleration or deceleration.

title: Machine learning classification of dynamical phases in a driven nonlinear Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures (3 in the main text, 4 in the appendices)
summary: Driven nonlinear photonic lattices can settle into steady, symmetry-broken, periodic, or chaotic states, and mapping where each occurs in parameter space is key to device design. Brute-force mapping is slow and relies on hand-built criteria, while machine-learning classifiers are usually tested on different systems, so it is unclear which suits a new lattice. We therefore apply four classifiers to the same coherently driven Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH) chain of Kerr resonators: a hand-built heuristic classifier based on Lyapunov exponents and spectral diagnostics, a supervised convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on the heuristic labels, an unsupervised library-building scheme based on augmented dynamic mode decomposition (aDMD), and an unsupervised Gaussian mixture model (GMM) on four dynamical invariants that include an aDMD reconstruction error. Using a converged heuristic diagram as the reference, the CNN reaches 98.0% held-out accuracy, while the two label-free methods reach adjusted Rand indices (ARIs) of 0.916 and 0.947, respectively, without seeing any labels. We show that the aDMD library cleanly resolves the stable and bistable phases and separates symmetric from symmetry-broken periodic oscillations, which the heuristic misses, though it cannot distinguish periodic from chaotic switching. We also find that a poorly converged reference understates the label-free methods' accuracy.

title: Non-axisymmetric MHD equilibria with an arbitrary number of field periods
summary: Several closed-form non-axisymmetric magnetic fields with nested toroidal flux surfaces have recently been discovered as exact benchmarks for verifying three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamic equilibrium codes. However, all of these solutions have at most two field periods ($N \le 2$), i.e., identical segments that repeat toroidally. Here, we derive closed-form non-axisymmetric magnetohydrodynamic equilibria for an arbitrary integer number of field periods $N \geq 1$. The equilibria have non-constant pressure and closed magnetic field lines with either zero rotational transform ($ι= 0$) for $N \geq 1$ or integer rotational transform ($ι= \pm N$) for $N \ge 3$. For the reflection-symmetric $ι= 0$ equilibria, we also construct a matched exterior vacuum field with continuous magnetic field across the plasma boundary, providing a benchmark for free-boundary equilibrium codes.

title: Equivariant Deep Learning in Direct-Product Space for Electronic-Structure Hamiltonian Prediction
summary: Most existing equivariant architectures for Hamiltonian prediction propagate features in direct-sum spaces of irreducible spherical tensors, whereas the target Hamiltonian is naturally an operator block in a direct-product representation over local orbital and spin bases. This representation mismatch fragments contiguous Hamiltonian blocks, obscures direct manipulation of orbital couplings, and organizes features into irregular angular-momentum components that require numerous transformations and are poorly aligned with efficient hardware execution and memory management. To address both the representation mismatch and computational bottleneck, we propose DP-Learner, an equivariant learning framework that performs message passing directly on Hamiltonian-like operator blocks in the direct-product space. Theoretically, we propose Lie-generator-based directional embedding and invariantly weighted left--right products and contractions that preserve equivariance to SO(3), SU(2), and spatial inversions, without explicit Clebsch--Gordan decomposition or inverse reconstruction. Methodologically, we instantiate this principle as a Transformer architecture, in which Hamiltonian-like feature matrices or tensors evolve through equivariant operators in the direct-product space, while non-linear invariant scalar routing controls structured gating over matrix units, directional propagation, attention, and environment-embedded context interactions. We further construct MP-HAM-110K, a large-scale Hamiltonian dataset comprising more than 110,000 material structures covering 68 elements with both Hamiltonian and wavefunction data. Experiments on MP-HAM-110K and Materials-HAM-SOC demonstrate that DP-Learner dramatically improves Hamiltonian prediction accuracy and inference efficiency over the state-of-the-art method.

title: Exascale-ready HemeLB for large-eddy simulation of full-human arterial blood flow
summary: Direct numerical simulation (DNS) of blood flow through the whole human arterial tree is limited by the number of lattice sites that must be advanced on a high-performance computer. We address this limit by combining the lattice Boltzmann solver HemeLB with Smagorinsky large-eddy simulation (LES). HemeLB runs with the same scaling behaviour on AMD, Intel and NVIDIA graphics processing units (GPUs) and sustains about 10 trillion lattice-site updates per second (TLUPS) on both the Frontier and Aurora exascale supercomputers. In stenotic aortic flow, LES on lattices five and ten times coarser than a 20~$μ$m DNS reproduces the wall pressure and the cross-sectional pressure and velocity, and its plane-averaged pressure differs from that of the DNS by at most 0.75~mmHg, below 1\% of the local pressure. At 100~$μ$m, LES reduces the estimated cost of a full-human simulation by a factor of about 625 relative to DNS. We use this resolution to compute blood flow from the head to the feet in a full-human arterial model with 295 million fluid sites, one inlet at the aortic root and 432 Windkessel outlets, at about 15--18 node-hours per cardiac cycle on two Frontier nodes. A single simulation resolves every region simultaneously, from the cerebral arteries to the arteries of the feet. The pressure pulse grows as it travels from the aorta to the feet, the shear stress concentrates in the branches rather than in the aorta, the pulse reaches the outlets later with increasing distance from the heart, and the flow in the legs and feet is triphasic, as in Doppler measurements of the human leg. These results bring patient-specific whole-body lattice Boltzmann simulations within reach of current supercomputers and pave the way for ensemble simulations towards a standard human model.

title: Analytical Modeling of the Admittance Tensor of Periodic Elliptical Meta-Atoms
summary: A metasurface is an electrically thin interface that controls the phase, amplitude and polarization of a wave, upon reflection or transmission. Printed on a grounded dielectric substrate and spatially modulated across the aperture, it converts a guided surface wave into a radiated leaky wave, a mechanism used in holographic metasurface antennas. Controlling this conversion requires synthesizing a prescribed distribution of admittance tensors, each derived from the homogenization of a subwavelength unit cell. Many numerical and semi-analytical methods have been proposed to relate the geometry of a meta-atom to the tensor it produces. This paper presents, to the author's knowledge, the first analytical model, restricted to elliptical meta-atoms on a uniform lattice. The Galerkin method is applied directly to the geometry of the patches, without spatial meshing. An affine transformation maps any rotated ellipse onto the unit disk, so that a single formulation covers every configuration. A wideband response takes from minutes to tens of minutes with a periodic full-wave solver, while the proposed model evaluates it in a few tens of milliseconds on the same workstation, roughly three orders of magnitude faster. The predicted admittance agrees with a method-of-moments reference up to the fundamental resonance and captures the guided-mode anomaly of the substrate. Beyond the physical insight it brings, the model is a differentiable function of the geometry, which makes the quasi-real-time design of optimized metasurfaces possible.

title: Suppression of the Laser Hosing Instability in a Parabolic Plasma Channel
summary: We present an analytical stability analysis of the laser hosing instability in a parabolic channel in the weakly relativistic regime. We employ a variational principle approach to derive a set of coupled equations describing laser dynamics in a transversely inhomogeneous plasma. The quadratic Lagrangian formalism is applied to perform a stability analysis and to derive the growth rates for hosing in both long- and short-wavelength regimes. We find that a parabolic channel suppresses the long-wavelength hosing mode completely, for any channel depth, and that the unstable band of the short-wavelength mode is bounded below by a cutoff wavenumber set by the ratio of the channel frequency to the hosing coupling. A steeper channel narrows the unstable band and lowers the short-wavelength growth rate, but cannot stabilize the mode, since the dispersion relation forbids damping identically. The analysis is accompanied by two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations, which reproduce the prediction in the nonlinear regime: the long-wavelength mode is absent in a channel, the surviving modulation shortens as the channel steepens, and its amplitude falls with channel depth. Further, our simulation results demonstrate the sensitivity of off-axis laser propagation to the plasma channel and distinguish the hosing instability from laser oscillations due to off-axis laser propagation in a plasma channel.

title: Simulation of Refraction Through Voxel Volumes
summary: Ray tracing in X-ray science has typically been limited to descriptions where refraction occurs only at interfaces, ignoring the refraction occurring due to the continuous variations in index of refraction in the bulk of a material, as are common in biological samples like bone. We propose a method to simulate X-ray images directly on voxel grids using curved rays. We first validate this method compared to a model with an analytical solution, and then investigate the effects of voxel size, interpolation choice, and illumination to grid alignment on a few simulated test objects. From these investigations, we make several recommendations to guide simulations using these techniques.

title: A continuum model of a diffusive compressible gas - Kinetic theory and real gases
summary: Using kinetic theory of gases, we derive the diffusive compressible Euler (dcE) model for ideal gases. The derivation covers all steps from the particle description of a gas, to macroscopic averages, to a discrete system of conservative balance equations in finite volumes, to the system of partial dif- ferential equations. Along the way, we discuss the modelling assumptions, and derive approximations of the diffusion coefficient. In the next part, we discuss the modifications needed to model real gases. In particular, we propose a tentative model for intermolecular friction forces.

title: An Agent-Driven, Cross-Validated Inverse-Design Pipeline for Dielectric Metasurfaces
comment: The code, are openly available on GitHub at \url{https://github.com/GiuseppeELio/metasurface-agent-pipeline} (MIT License) and archived on Zenodo at 10.5281/zenodo.23982523
summary: Inverse design of dielectric metasurfaces is powerful but labour-intensive: each new target requires choosing a parameterization and a figure of merit, managing compute resources, and critically assessing results that may be numerically unconverged, sensitive to fabrication errors or trapped in local optima. Here we present an open-source pipeline in which an artificial intelligence (AI) coding agent turns a plain-language specification into metasurface optimization runs, executes them, analyses every run with a fixed checklist and proposes the next iteration. Designs are optimized with differentiable three-dimensional rigorous coupled-wave analysis (RCWA), including robustness to fabrication tolerances, and every reported design is independently verified with finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations. We demonstrate the workflow at 1550 nm on a freeform silicon metagrating, on a polarization-independent meta-atom library assembled into beam-deflecting supercells, and on metalenses built from the same library. In the metagrating case, the independent FDTD verification revealed a 5\% overestimate of the efficiency by the optimization model that a conventional convergence test had not detected, and the robust design retained most of its efficiency under $\pm$10~nm fabrication errors. In the other cases, instead, the obtained RCWA results are confirmed by full-wave simulations.

title: The dielectric tensor for a fully anisotropic regularized Kappa plasma
summary: It has been known for some decades that the plasma in the Solar System is invariably in a state away from thermal equilibrium. In several plasma environments, be it in the Solar Wind or within planetary magnetospheres, the plasma has been found in a quasi-stationary nonthermal state, with a substantial fraction of its high-energy particles fitting along power-law distributions, instead of the exponential decay of thermal systems. Translating the observations in energy to velocity distribution functions (VDFs), the Kappa plasma model has been employed by the space plasma community, with the (standard) Kappa VDF (SKD) being the preferred choice. However, recent works have called attention to the limitations of the SKD model, proposing as a viable alternative the regularized Kappa VDF (RKD) model, which corrects the deficiencies of the SKD. The RKD model introduces a Gaussian-like dependency on the very high-energy part of the VDF that effectively cut-offs, via a regularization parameter, the Lorentzian profile of the intermediate-energy range. In this work, we employ a generalized RKD that supports anisotropies both in the thermal speed parameters and in the regularization parameters, including as well the possibility of drifts parallel to the magnetic field. This generalized RKD (called the bi-regularized Kappa with drift distribution, bRKd), is employed to derive for the first time the components of the susceptibility tensor for a suprathermal plasma species/population modelled by the bRKd. The tensor components are valid for waves with any propagation angle, frequency range and polarization. During the derivation, new special functions are defined and analyzed, which generalize previous expressions restricted to the parallel propagation limit.

title: Projection-based segregated, iterative, and multi-stage physics-informed neural network for incompressible Navier-stokes equations
summary: Physics-informed neural networks(PINNs) offer a mesh-free and continuously differentiable approach to fluid simulation. However, standard monolithic PINNs for incompressible Navier-Stokes (NS) equations often suffer from severe constraint coupling and spectral biases, limiting both convergence and accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a segregated, iterative, and multi-stage PINN (SIM-PINN) inspired by the classical projection method in computational fluid dynamics. In SIM-PINN, the nonlinear NS equations are decoupled into the linearized momentum and pressure Poisson equations. Each is addressed separately using dedicated multi-stage neural networks and coupled through projection-based inner iterations. Each stage of the multi-stage neural networks for the momentum equations corresponds to one iteration of the projection method, in which the velocity fields are progressively refined at targeted frequencies. Upon iteration convergence, solutions to the fully coupled and nonlinear NS equations are recovered. By integrating the segregated and iterative framework with the multi-stage training, SIM-PINN alleviates the optimization difficulties of the incompressible NS equations arising from nonlinearity, constraint coupling, and spectral biases. The improved convergence and accuracy are demonstrated by simulations of steady lid-driven cavity and unsteady Kolmogorov flows.

title: Vibration patterns and reed - pipe coupling in the free reeds of the hulusi
summary: The hulusi is a free-reed instrument from Yunnan, Western China, known for its unique sound. Its reed and frame are cut from a single brass sheet in a symmetric shape, the free end narrower than the clamped end. Its free reeds are coupled to tubes that determine the instrument's pitch during normal playing. With reduced playing pressure, the reed frequency takes over the instrument sound. We report point-by-point laser Doppler vibrometry on the reeds of six handmade hulusi, two each in the keys of F, B$\flat$ and C, measured at 29 points on every reed or tongue over nine fingerings and two supply pressures. Steady-state spectra carry two components: a tube-dominant frequency $f_\mathrm{tube}$, locked to the air-column resonance and carrying a complete harmonic series, and a reed-dominant frequency $f_\mathrm{reed}$, which is not an integer multiple of it. Their difference $Δ= f_\mathrm{tube} - f_\mathrm{reed}$ runs from 38 to 523~Hz across the dataset, from about three semitones to more than an octave. The reed-dominant frequency rises with the pressure at the reed, by $28.0 \pm 10.3$ Hz/kPa once $f_\mathrm{tube}$ is controlled for. At low pressure supply the oscillation loses its lock to the air column, falls silent for about 100~ms, and returns at the reed frequency within 0.1 Hz. The spatial patterns are forced oscillation shapes of one limit cycle at its fundamental and harmonics rather than eigenmodes: the measured frequencies stand in strict 1:2:3 ratios, far from the bending ratios of a cantilever. The reed-dominant pattern is pure bending and holds across fingerings and supply pressures, whereas the tube-dominant pattern breaks up near the oscillation threshold.

title: Goos-Hänchen Shifts at 458 nm from DUV Dichroic Laser Mirrors
summary: We report polarization- and angle-dependent lateral beam shifts observed at 458~nm upon reflection from a deep-ultraviolet (DUV) dichroic multilayer mirror. These Goos--Hänchen (GH) shifts originate from the phase of the complex Fresnel reflection coefficient and are quantitatively reproduced using a transfer-matrix model. Simultaneous reflectance (R), transmittance (T), and GH shift measurements provide complementary constraints on the coating's amplitude and phase response. The analysis is extended to transmission, predicting analogous phase-induced lateral shifts. In frequency-doubling cavities using dichroic mirrors, these phase effects can accumulate over multiple reflections, leading to deviations from ray-optics predictions that may affect cavity mode structure and resonance conditions. Our results show a GH shift of as much as 2~\textmu m (\bm{$\approx 4.4λ$}), which, combined with RT data, enables improved characterization of the phase response of the multilayer coating. The p-polarized reflectance is minimized at a pseudo-Brewster angle of \bm{$θ_B \approx 46^\circ$} at 458~nm, providing a natural reference point around which the GH shift is enhanced.

title: The shear Alfvén continuum of optimized stellarators
summary: The shear Alfvén continuum has been studied extensively in tokamaks, but its gap structure in modern optimized stellarators has received less attention, despite its importance for energetic-particle confinement in fusion pilot plants. We compute and compare the continua of five reactor-scale stellarator equilibria: two quasi-axisymmetric (QA), two quasi-helically symmetric (QH), and one quasi-isodynamic (QI). We present selective Fourier mode schemes that provide a sufficient resolution of eigenfrequencies within the frequency range of interest. In all five configurations, the widest gap is the HAE(2,$N_{\text{fp}}$) gap, which is driven by rotating ellipticity. This gap lies in the frequency range of strong resonance with prompt fusion-born alphas in the QA configurations but not in the QH configurations, suggesting that QH configurations may be easier to optimize for alpha confinement. Near-axis theory predicts the HAE(2,$N_{\text{fp}}$) and EAE gap widths well but overestimates the MAE gap widths and the gap widths of the QI configuration. These discrepancies likely arise from interactions between gaps, which depend on the rotational transform profile and are not captured by near-axis theory.

title: Energy-conserving scheme for a shallow-water model with capillary effects
summary: We consider numerical approximations of shallow-water and thin-film flow models with capillary effects. These models lead to third-order differential equations, and we work with an augmented model with second-order derivatives. For a wide class of such models, which includes the classical shallow-water model and thin-film flow models, we develop a fully discrete energy-conserving scheme for both the quadratic and fully nonlinear capillary models. Numerical results show that the proposed scheme is stable and conserves total energy in the absence of dissipative effects.

title: Extracting Single-Mode Rayleigh--Taylor Instability dynamics from data via SINDy
summary: Rayleigh-Taylor instability (RTI) is of fundamental importance in fields such as inertial confinement fusion and supernova explosions, and its evolution is commonly described by potential--flow theory and buoyancy--drag models. However, both types of models struggle to accurately capture the overshoot behavior of bubble and spike velocities, as well as the subsequent reacceleration stage. To address these limitations, we develop a physics-constrained, data-driven framework based on the integral formulation of Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics (SINDy), which extracts low-dimensional dynamical equations for bubble and spike evolution directly from data. By introducing the nondimensional initial amplitude $A_0 = kη_0$ as an explicit parameter, we identify distinct dynamical equations for the bubble and the spike based on data spanning multiple Atwood numbers and initial amplitudes. The resulting low-dimensional dynamical equations not only reproduce the overshoot behavior of the velocity with good accuracy, but also capture the reacceleration stage well, while maintaining high predictive accuracy at unseen values of the wavenumber, acceleration, and Atwood number. This work provides a physics-constrained, data-driven framework complementary to conventional potential-flow and buoyancy--drag models, accurately describing the dynamical evolution of the bubble and spike at high Atwood numbers, and provides a new perspective for directly extracting the dynamical equations of interfacial instabilities from data.

title: Characterization and Suppression of Parasitic Back-Reflection Noise in Transponder-Type Heterodyne Interferometry
summary: Transponder-type heterodyne interferometry is a versatile metrological technique for high-precision measurements, with applications in Earth's gravity-field recovery, space-based gravitational-wave detection, deep-space ranging, and Doppler tracking. However, parasitic back-reflections can contaminate phase readout and degrade measurement sensitivity. To characterize and suppress this noise, we constructed a transponder-type interferometer with coaxially aligned counter-propagating beams, achieving stable operation at a received optical power of 720 pW. An adjustable reflecting system was introduced into the master-side transmit path to simulate back-reflection under realistic conditions. Optical path scans and model fitting showed that phase errors vary periodically with the relative phase between the main and parasitic interference signals, which defines the working point. Assisted by π measurement, adjustment to low-sensitivity working points was combined with balanced detection to suppress back-reflection phase noise, achieving maximum suppression factors of 77 for single-frequency phase errors and 23 for band-limited phase-noise amplitude spectral density. π measurement also enabled working point diagnosis at 3.8 nW back-reflection power, confirming its applicability under weak back-reflection conditions. These results provide an effective approach for in situ back-reflection characterization and phase-noise suppression in transponder-type heterodyne interferometry.

title: Eddies that ride the flow: a model of turbulence with Richardson dispersion and anomalous dissipation
comment: The code, the analysis scripts that produce every figure and numbers in the paper, the run configurations, the data behind the figures and the supplementary movies are available at https://github.com/R1967J/kinematic-field. A single self-contained generator of the velocity field kinematic_field.py
summary: We construct a divergence-free velocity field $\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x},t)$ on $\mathbb{T}^{n}$ that is a genuine function of position and carries both defining properties of turbulent transport: Richardson pair dispersion and a dissipative anomaly. No synthetic field has carried both, because the frame that gives the first destroys the field the second requires. The key is a dichotomy: deforming a spectrally localised pattern smears it across scales, whereas pushing its generating centres forward and re-convolving leaves the spectral envelope exactly invariant --- so transporting the eddy centres preserves both cascade and frame. In the field the finite-size Lyapunov exponent obeys $ζ(R)=h(R)-1$ threshold by threshold within the scaling range, with a sweeping deficit $Δ_{\rm sw}=+0.038\pm0.019$, consistent with zero, against $+0.091\pm0.019$ for the frozen field on the same data, a gap that doubles at Navier--Stokes intermittency. Companion papers prove that this family shows Richardson dispersion and a dissipative anomaly (Fefferman and Mayboroda 2026), and that a scalar advected by this flow obeys Yaglom's relation (De Lellis 2026), at small Kubo number. Trajectories forget their starting point as the smallest eddy is removed: the median separation of pairs released from one point with independent Brownian kicks varies as $κ_{p}^{0.0333\pm0.0038}$ over 22 decades of particle diffusivity, against $κ_{p}^{1/2}$ for a smooth control. A scalar in the same field closes the exact scale-by-scale variance budget, four independently measured terms balancing the dissipation to 15\% over 1.2 decades with no adjustable constant, and reaches its inertial--convective asymptote $S_{L}=-χr$ to $0.9995\pm0.0018$ once the measured diffusive transfer is restored, while under an imposed mean gradient $χ$ changes by 14\% over a factor 5.8 in $κ$.

title: Improving the accuracy of the momentum-exchange method in lattice Boltzmann methods
summary:
In the lattice Boltzmann method (LBM), the momentum-exchange method (MEM) is widely used to evaluate hydrodynamic forces at fluid-solid interfaces due to its computational efficiency and geometric flexibility. However, when mapping complex geometries onto structured Cartesian grids, the physical boundary rarely intersects the lattice links exactly at their midpoints. This discrepancy violates an implicit assumption inherent to the conventional momentum-exchange (CME) formulation. In this study, we systematically analyze this geometric deficiency and demonstrate that it induces significant force inaccuracies, even in elementary flows where the solid boundary deviates from the midway position. To resolve this, we propose a modified momentum-exchange (MME) method that explicitly accounts for the exact boundary location along the lattice links, demonstrating enhanced accuracy for both flat and curved geometries.
  Furthermore, we address another critical issue with the interpolation-supplemented bounce-back (ISBB) schemes, and that is their inherent violation of local mass conservation. This mass leakage induces unphysical pressure buildup in the system, which compromises the accuracy and stability of the LBM. We propose a mass-conservative remedy for ISBB schemes that eliminates this leakage. Through a series of benchmark simulations of increasing complexity, we demonstrate that combining the proposed MME with the mass-corrected ISBB scheme drastically improves the fidelity of hydrodynamic force evaluations, establishing a robust framework essential for moving boundary problems and fluid-structure interactions.

title: Bayesian Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for trustworthy Reynolds-stress closures
summary: Data-driven turbulence closures can improve Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) predictions, but their use is limited by two issues: learned constitutive relations are often difficult to inspect, and predictions typically lack reliable uncertainty estimates. We develop a Bayesian tensor-basis Kolmogorov-Arnold network (BKAN) for Reynolds-stress anisotropy that addresses both within a single closure. Learnable univariate spline functions on network edges provide an inspectable representation that can, where sufficiently simple, be approximated symbolically. Variational posteriors over spline coefficients yield a predictive distribution separating epistemic uncertainty, due to limited training data, from aleatoric uncertainty, the irreducible scatter of high-fidelity targets at given inputs. Galilean and rotational invariance, symmetry, and tracelessness are enforced through the tensor basis, while physical realisability is treated separately through soft regularisation. A controlled regression benchmark assesses predictive accuracy, calibration, and Bayesian parameterisation. Placing the posterior on spline coefficients gives the best overall balance of accuracy, calibration, parameter cost, and interpretability. Applied to Reynolds-stress anisotropy, the BKAN is accurate in distribution, with calibrated, informative uncertainty that tends to identify larger prediction errors. Under geometric extrapolation, however, the model becomes overconfident: epistemic uncertainty increases but does not fully account for growing prediction errors. Finally, the framework is extended to three-dimensional wind-farm wakes, where the learned correction transfers to unseen layouts and posterior samples are propagated through the RANS solver, with the aleatoric component injected as a spatially correlated field, to obtain uncertainty bounds on the predicted wake flow.

title: Photonic Exceptional Topological Bound States in the Continuum
summary: Exceptional bound states in the continuum (EBICs) arise when bound states in the continuum (BICs) with distinct intrinsic losses coalesce at exceptional points (EPs), combining continuum-embedded wave confinement with a non-analytic spectral response. However, conventional EBICs rely on precisely controlled modal coupling and intrinsic loss, making them fragile and difficult to realize experimentally. Here, we introduce bulk-band topology to mitigate this fragility and experimentally realize a photonic exceptional topological BIC (ETBIC) in spoof surface plasmon polariton waveguides by merging two symmetry-protected topological BICs (TBICs) to coalesce at an EP, with the topological design supporting robust localization under symmetry-preserving perturbations. By engineering an intrinsic loss contrast and tuning the intermodal coupling, we directly resolve the coalescence of the complex eigenfrequencies, accompanied by measured near-field distributions consistent with the exceptional eigenstate. Furthermore, weak perturbations induce approximately square-root eigenfrequency splitting, yielding an enhanced spectral response compared with the approximately linear frequency shift of an isolated TBIC. These results establish bulk-band topology as a design principle for exceptional BIC engineering and provide a foundation for EBIC-based photonic sensing.

title: A physics-based adaptive low-rank method for 6D Vlasov simulations
summary: The numerical simulation of kinetic plasma models in six-dimensional phase space poses significant computational and memory challenges, particularly when considering modern high-performance computing architectures. In this work, we propose an adaptive dynamical low-rank approach for the efficient solution of the 6D Vlasov--Poisson system. Our strategy is an extension of the projector-splitting dynamical low-rank integrator. The algorithm changes the rank based on physical observables (e.g., the electric field and energy) as opposed to controlling the error in the distribution function. Our approach is memory efficient in the sense that only rank $r$ objects are required to implement the scheme. This makes the algorithm suitable for performing high-dimensional computations on graphic processing units. Comparisons with rank adaptive Basis-Update & Galerkin integrators exhibit both significant memory savings and reduction in run time. We show, by presenting a variety of 6D benchmark experiments implemented in the C++/CUDA low-rank framework Ensign, that our technique allows us to run simulations with a significantly smaller rank, while still preserving the physical fidelity. Thus, the approach substantially reduces memory footprint and computational cost and enables simulations that are prohibitively expensive for full-rank or less memory-efficient low-rank schemes.

title: Field-aligned measurement removes the anisotropy barrier of sample-based quantum subspace solvers for magnetized-plasma heat conduction
summary: Sample-based quantum subspace methods construct a small subspace from measured basis states and solve the target problem classically within it. We study these methods for heat conduction in magnetized plasmas, where the anisotropy $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp$ reaches $10^8$ to $10^{10}$. We prove two results for the energy-norm Galerkin solution. First, if the measurement basis is aligned with the flux surfaces and the subspace contains the poloidal-mode-zero block, the error is bounded by $\|r_0\|_{L^+}(χ_\parallel-χ_\perp)^{-1/2}$, where the numerator does not depend on $χ_\parallel$. The bound is sharp, so the accuracy improves as the anisotropy grows. Second, in the computational basis, a subspace that misses a single node of a flux surface suppresses the flux-function component there as $χ_\parallel^{-1/2}$, which gives an error floor when the limiting solution is nonzero on that surface. We verify both results on a shaped cross-section and on a KSTAR-like Miller equilibrium with ten qubits. At $χ_\parallel/χ_\perp=10^9$, the computational basis gives an error of order unity for every shot budget, whereas a quantum Fourier transform on the poloidal register gives $1.3\times10^{-5}$. The same barrier limits sample-based quantum diagonalization. The aligned measurement needs no time evolution, so the circuit is only state preparation and a five-qubit quantum Fourier transform. On a ten-qubit superconducting processor, the aligned basis gives a median error of $7.0\times10^{-6}$ with 768 shots, whereas the computational basis gives errors above 0.94 up to $1.2\times10^4$ shots. A trapped-ion processor shows the same behavior.

title: Convection in the interior of Cepheid variable stars
comment: Accepted for publication in Physical Review Fluids. This paper is associated with a poster winner of a 2025 APS DFD Gallery of Fluid Motion Award
summary: This paper is associated with a poster winner of a 2025 American Physical Society's Division of Fluid Dynamics (DFD) Gallery of Fluid Motion Award for work presented at the DFD Gallery of Fluid Motion. The original poster is available online at the Gallery of Fluid Motion, https://doi.org/10.1103/APS.DFD.2025.GFM.P005.

title: Thermal Inverse Design: Tailoring the Transient Response of Resistive Micro-Heaters
summary: Microheaters underpin a broad range of applications that require localized and dynamic thermal control. Engineering their spatial and temporal temperature distributions is therefore essential, yet conventional heater design relies largely on iterative trial and error involving numerous full-scale thermal simulations. Here, we introduce an inverse design algorithm for pulsed heating, a common operating modality in thermal processing, sensing, switching, and material characterization. The approach uses a single lithographic step to pattern the doped regions of a silicon microheater and, in principle, enables on-demand peak temperature distributions under transient voltage excitation within one closed design loop. The algorithm also incorporates practical fabrication constraints, including finite lithographic resolution. We demonstrate its versatility through three representative designs. First, an optimized heater achieves more than a 20-fold reduction in temperature nonuniformity compared with a conventional uniformly doped heater. Second, inverse-designed doping effectively cancels the thermal gradient in a heater connected in series with a diode. Third, the method generates prescribed linear temperature gradients on demand. These results establish inverse-designed doping as a scalable and fabrication-compatible approach for tailoring transient temperature distributions in resistive microheaters.

title: A hierarchy of physics-embedded neural operators for structural dynamic surrogate modelingA hierarchy of physics-embedded neural operators for structural dynamic surrogate modeling
summary: Structural-response surrogates must capture moving resonances, phase changes, and unequal-amplitude transfer channels during optimization or health-state changes. Physics-embedded learning seeks FEA-level accuracy at lower cost by embedding physics in inputs, forward passes, losses, and backpropagation. We propose Modal Rational (MR), mapping structural features to modal quantities for analytical frequency-response reconstruction. The Physics-Guided Modal Operator Network (PGMON) adds bounded frequency, damping, and residual-flexibility corrections. Modal Operator with Structural GELU and Anchored-SIREN Correction (MOSAIC) denotes the bounded spectral-discrepancy framework used here; MOSAIC-MR and MOSAIC-PGMON add such discrepancies. They support finite-dimensional maps and physical decoders for future neural operators; evidence is fixed-topology, not a completed operator comparison. Two 20,000-design populations are studied: an 80 m steel truss tower with variable member areas and attached masses, and a tapered shell beam with ten variable station masses. Archived tests cover ten designs and seven acceleration histories per structure; they are benchmarks, not seismic-design assessments. With 5% reference modal damping, MR, PGMON, and MOSAIC give mean displacement-history errors of 0.73-0.76% for the tower and 0.029-0.116% for the beam, against declared band-limited modal references. Supplied modal frequencies are distinguished from design-only use; unequal parameter counts and training settings are explicit. Error analysis separates learned modal discrepancies, truncation, and excitation weighting, explaining acceleration and difficult-tower limits and risks of blind use. Results support physically structured prediction but limit claims about generalization, computational savings, and added corrections. Next is developing and validating neural operators around these architectures.

title: Novel hydrodynamic features in dissipative spin-polarized fluids
summary: We investigate an extension of perfect spin hydrodynamics that includes dissipation in the spin sector. The presence of dissipation implies that antisymmetric parts of the energy-momentum tensor should be taken into account. Their form follows from the Navier-Stokes or Israel-Stewart theory, which introduces a priori unknown kinetic coefficients and relaxation times. We find that the inclusion of the antisymmetric parts of the energy-momentum tensor has twofold effects: i) they form source terms for the spin tensor allowing for the transfer between the spin and orbital parts of the total angular momentum (spin-orbit interaction) and ii) they appear in the conservation laws for the energy and linear momentum, indirectly affecting the spin dynamics. Numerical results are obtained for two boost-invariant expansion geometries: one-dimensional longitudinal motion (Bjorken model) and two-dimensional boost-invariant and cylindrically symmetric expansion. They indicate (for various choices of the spin kinetic coefficients and the relaxation times) that the spin polarization tensor approaches thermal vorticity. We also observe that Israel-Stewart dynamics on the way to local equilibrium approaches first the Navier-Stokes regime. In general, we find that the Israel-Stewart formalism naturally helps to consistently combine the conservation laws for linear and angular momentum, while the Navier-Stokes framework itself can lead to a disruption in the structure of the equations through the inclusion of terms involving derivatives of an order higher than one.

title: Hybrid integration of a SESAM with a silicon nitride photonic integrated circuit
summary: The realization of high-performance femtosecond lasers on photonic integrated circuits (PICs) requires robust, low-loss coupling between a saturable absorber and a photonic waveguide. In this work, we demonstrate the hybrid integration of a semiconductor saturable absorber mirror (SESAM) with a silicon nitride (SiN) PIC by micro-assembly. This micro-assembly strategy transfers the non-linear functionality of the absorber onto the PIC. We characterize the linear and non-linear performance of an unbonded SESAM and of a SESAM bonded to inverse-tapered SiN waveguides. At 1560~nm, the bonded device shows a waveguide-coupled modulation depth of 5.2\%, a maximum reflectivity of 37.2\%, and a saturation fluence of 47~\textmu J/cm$^2$. This work demonstrates that SESAMs can be integrated directly onto silicon nitride-based PIC platforms and provides a pathway towards fully integrated, self-starting, chip-scale ultrafast lasers.

title: A characteristic mapping method for dissipative evolution equations
summary: The Characteristic Mapping (CM) method is a transport scheme which discretizes the Lagrangian flow map as a composition of spatial interpolants. This adaptive approximation technique has demonstrated novel resolution properties and the ability to efficiently simulate the fine scales of inviscid turbulent flows. In this work, we construct an extension of this approach to the solution of dissipative problems, including the Navier-Stokes equations. The extension lifts a general scalar evolution equation to a path in a group of diffeomorphisms, where the semigroup approach of the CM method can be exploited. We give an interpretation of this lift through the geometric framework of optimal transport. We then introduce a semidirect product evolution technique to perform the time stepping of the map components. The map is evolved based on the semi-Lagrangian CM approach, and its log-Jacobian is evolved explicitly by an exponential integrator. The numerical scheme is demonstrated to be high-order accurate and is tested on a range of canonical nonlinear dissipative equations.
